title: A negative support weight obstructs integrality over a monoid algebra
statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $H$ be a finitely generated torsion-free abelian group, let $P\subseteq H$ be a submonoid, and let $w:H\to\mathbf Z$ be a group homomorphism with $w(p)\ge0$ for every $p\in P$. Let $x=\sum_{g\in S}c_ge^g\in k[H]$ be nonzero with finite support. If some $g\in S$ has $w(g)<0$, then $x$ is not integral over $k[P]$. Here $k[P]$ and $k[H]$ use the additive monoid and group-algebra conventions of [def-trf-fine-fan-blowup].

source.place: Expose VIII, Lemma 3.2.9 and the monomial-basis normalization argument, printed p.104; the least-weight argument is expanded here.

proof.text: Write $k[H]=\bigoplus_{h\in H}ke^h$, with coefficientwise addition and $e^he^{h'}=e^{h+h'}$. The monomial map $k[P]\to k[H]$ is injective: the coefficient at $p\in P$ after applying it is the original coefficient at $p$. For an integer $d$, let $[f]_d=\sum_{w(h)=d}f_he^h$ for a finite sum $f$; this operation is additive. Since $S$ is the actual support of $x\ne0$, it is finite and nonempty. Put $m=\min_{g\in S}w(g)$ and $y=[x]_m$. Then $m<0$ by the hypothesis, $y\ne0$ since it retains a nonzero coefficient attaining the minimum, and every exponent of $y$ has weight $m$.

source.place: Expose VIII, 3.2.8--3.2.9 and Lemma 3.2.12 first proof paragraph, printed p.104; explicit least-weight argument supplied by the agent (not a proof quoted from ILO).

proof.text:
To justify non-cancellation, choose finite group generators $h_1,\ldots,h_r$ of $H$ and let $Q$ be the submonoid generated by $h_1,-h_1,\ldots,h_r,-h_r$. Every integer combination of the $h_j$ is a sum of these generators with nonnegative integer coefficients, so $Q=H$ as subsets of $H$. Thus $Q$ is a finitely generated submonoid generating the torsion-free abelian group $H$. Apply [lem-trf-monoid-algebra-domain-fraction] with $G=H$ and this $Q$: its domain clause says that $k[H]$ is an integral domain. Consequently $y^j

proof.text: For every $j\ge0$, all support exponents of $x^j$ have weight at least $jm$, and $[x^j]_{jm}=y^j$. Here is the finite-convolution induction, including its base: $x^0=1=e^0$, with weight $0$ and component $1=y^0$. For the step, expand $x^jx$ using pairs $a\in\operatorname{supp}(x^j)$ and $b\in S$. Every pair has $w(a+b)=w(a)+w(b)\ge jm+m$. If $w(a+b)=(j+1)m$, equality forces $w(a)=jm$ and $w(b)=m$ since both summands have these lower bounds. Thus, for each exponent of weight $(j+1)m$, its coefficient in $x^{j+1}$ is exactly the coefficient in $[x^j]_{jm}[x]_m=y^jy=y^{j+1}$. The latter product has only weight $(j+1)m$ by additivity of $w$, which proves the component identity. Summing coefficients can remove exponents, but cannot create any below the bound. By step 2 the displayed component $y^j$ is nonzero.

source.place: Expose VIII, 3.2.8--3.2.9 and Lemma 3.2.12 first proof paragraph, printed p.104; explicit least-weight argument supplied by the agent (not a proof quoted from ILO).

proof.text: Suppose $x$ were integral over $k[P]$. By the definition of integrality, there would be a monic equation $x^n+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_ix^i=0$ with $a_i\in k[P]$. Its degree $n$ is positive: a monic constant polynomial is $1$, whose value is nonzero in $k[H]$. Every support exponent $p$ of $a_i$ belongs to $P$ and has $w(p)\ge0$. Expanding $a_ix^i$ coefficientwise, every exponent that remains has weight at least $im$, by step 3. For $i<n$ and $m<0$ one has $im>nm$, so $[a_ix^i]_{nm}=0$ (also when $a_i=0$). Apply the additive operation $[\,\cdot\,]_{nm}$ to the equation. Step 3 gives $0=[x^n]_{nm}+\sum_{i<n}[a_ix^i]_{nm}=y^n$, contradicting step 2. Hence $x$ is not integral over $k[P]$.
